 137:   `.collab/<task>/sessions.json`, never the task's newest thread overall. With a roster,
 138:   the thread's own ledger entry decides the reviewer.
 139: - `-Model <name>` â€” omit it and the model comes from the roster entry used, else the top
 140:   level of the user's `~/.codex/config.toml`; the resolved model is always pinned with
 141:   `-m`. Only pass it when the user asked for a specific model.
 142: - `-Provider <name>` â€” a `[model_providers.<name>]` entry from the Codex config
 143:   (case-sensitive), for consulting one specific reviewer (e.g. GLM through a z.ai
 144:   provider entry). Needs `-Model` alongside it unless that provider's roster entry names
 145:   a model. **A second model is consulted in its own lineage; never
 146:   fork/resume across providers** â€” the bridge enforces this by refusing a `-Thread`
 147:   or automatic parent whose lineage does not match the current `-Provider`/`-Model`,
 148:   but do not try to work around that by hand either. See the README sections "Reviewer
 149:   identity and lineage", "Effort vocabularies (caps-v1)" and "Peak-hour windows" for how
 150:   the provider is resolved, the effort vocabulary per endpoint, and peak-hour handling.
 151:   A ledger entry from a 0.1/0.2 task
 152:   carries no reviewer identity, so its provenance is unknown: the first 0.3.0
 153:   consultation on such a task always starts a new thread, whatever provider or model
 154:   you use.
 155: - `-Engine codex|agy|muse` â€” the CLI that carries the consultation (0.4.0). Omitted, it comes
 156:   from the roster entry used (`"engine": "agy"` for Gemini through Google's Antigravity CLI),
 157:   else `codex`. For agy, `-Provider` is a free label (e.g. `gemini`) and `-Model` the full
 158:   model id with its tier (`gemini-3.8-flash-high`); no effort is sent (the tier is in the
 159:   id), the default mode is `new` (`-Mode resume` / `-Thread` continue a conversation), and
 160:   `fork`, `-Sandbox workspace-write`, `-CodexConfig` and `-SchemaTransport output-schema`
 161:   are refused. Its files are `handoffs/<NN>-agy-<slug>.*`. An agy run FAILS when the working
 162:   tree (tracked or untracked files) or the collab directory (every task's stores and
 163:   handoffs) changed during it, by the reviewer or anyone else (agy's sandbox does not block
 164:   writes) - do not edit the repository or the collab directory, and run no other
 165:   consultation here, while one runs. Read-only is enforced by evidence for tracked and
 166:   untracked files and the collab directory; not for gitignored paths, submodules or files
 167:   outside the repository. `-DenialRetry 0|1` (default 1): one more turn when a tool was
 168:   auto-denied and the turn produced nothing. `-EngineExe <path>` if `agy` is not on `PATH`.
 169:   `-Provider gemini` without `-Model` on a roster with several `gemini` entries takes the
 170:   first one and warns (`roster: label gemini names 2 entries; ...`) - pass `-Model` for
 171:   another. See the README section "Engines". `muse` (wave 23: Meta's Muse Code CLI for the
 172:   Muse Code subscription; `"engine": "muse"`, label e.g. `meta`, `-Model muse-spark-1.3` or
 173:   `muse-spark-1.3-contributor`): the effort goes as `--reasoning-effort`; the default mode is
 174:   `new`; files `handoffs/<NN>-muse-<slug>.*`; no denial retry; `-MaxModelSteps <n>` caps its
 175:   model steps (muse only). A muse run is REFUSED while `META_API_KEY` or `MODEL_API_KEY` is
 176:   set (it would bill per token), and while no oauth sign-in is established (the keychain
 177:   backend, no `auth.json`, no mechanism: `the Muse sign-in is not established as oauth
 178:   (<cause>): ...`) - also under `-SkipPreflight`, in the roster walk and in a panel; never set
 179:   or unset those variables and never sign in yourself, tell the user (`TBH_CREDENTIAL_BACKEND=file`,
 180:   then `muse login`). Its sign-in is `~/.config/muse/auth.json`; never read that file. The same read-only tree
 181:   check as agy applies. `-EngineExe <path>` names the launcher of the selected engine
 182:   (`-Engine`'s, else the roster's only engine other than codex).
 183: - `-NativeEffort <value>` â€” send an effort value verbatim when the resolved provider's
 184:   endpoint has no known vocabulary (the run refuses `-Effort` in that case and tells you
 185:   to use this instead).
 186: - `-OffPeakOnly` â€” refuse the run instead of just warning when the provider's peak-hour
 187:   window (`CODEX_CONSULT_PEAK_<PROVIDER>`) is active, or when no schedule is set for it.
 188: - `-SkipPreflight` â€” bypass the automatic preflight (the bridge otherwise refuses,
 189:   before the lock, a provider whose credentials are missing, whose availability cannot
 190:   be established, whose endpoint was rejected as unauthenticated in the last 24 h, or
 191:   whose usage limit resets in the future; with a roster, the first entry is then taken
 192:   unchecked). Only for an endpoint that genuinely needs no credential, or once after the
 193:   user rotated a credential â€” do not use it to push past a real refusal.
 194: - `-CodexConfig key=value[,â€¦]` â€” pass extra `-c` overrides straight through to `codex
 195:   exec`. The bridge refuses any key it already owns (`model`, `model_provider`,
 196:   `model_reasoning_effort`, `profile`, `model_providers(.*)`). Example: a
 197:   `[model_providers.mimo]` entry (Xiaomi MiMo) needs its model catalog supplied per run
 198:   rather than set globally in the user's Codex config, since a global
 199:   `model_catalog_json` replaces Codex's own catalog and can degrade an unrelated
 200:   model â€” `-CodexConfig model_catalog_json=~/.codex/model-catalogs.json`.
 201: - `-Purpose <purpose>` (see table above), `-Effort low|medium|high|xhigh`,
 202:   `-MaxWords <n>` (both override the preset), `-TimeoutSec <n>` (0.5.0: default the
 203:   purpose's - chore 600, checkpoint and none 900, framing and decision 1800, diff-review,
 204:   core-contract and stuck 2400, acceptance 3600 s), `-Sandbox read-only|workspace-write`
 205:   (default `read-only`).
 206: - **A big review** (0.5.0): pass `-Range <from>..<to>` (two revisions: `base..head` or
 207:   `base...head`; a single revision is refused) with diff-review and acceptance
 208:   (the bridge measures it with `git diff --shortstat`, tells the reviewer its size and
 209:   WARNS when more than 1500 lines meet a timeout below 2400 s) and/or `-TimeoutSec`, or give
 210:   the brief a reading plan (which files first, what to skip). Never leave a big review to
 211:   the 900 s of a checkpoint. **The acceptance of a big change: write `-TimeoutSec 3600` into the
 212:   brief's command** - explicitly, although `acceptance` defaults to it: the command then says
 213:   what the run was given, and a changed default or another purpose cannot shrink it (an 1800 s
 214:   limit timed out three acceptance reviewers of one big change in practice).
 215: - A reviewer killed on its timeout gets ONE continuation turn on its own thread (`-ContinueSec
 216:   <s>`, default min(timeout, 900); `0` = off): usable -> `usable reply (after a timeout
 217:   continuation)`, ingested like any reply - but only when it passes a first reply's checks (a
 218:   valid object or substantive prose; a `Done.` is `failed: not a usable reply - ...` and the
 219:   salvage is kept). No continuation when files changed during the run or the killed turn
 220:   reported a quota, billing or auth failure. If it fails too, the summary prints a
 221:   `partial    :` line (the salvaged `handoffs/<NN>-<engine>-<slug>.partial.md`: what the
 222:   reviewer produced before the kill) and `resume     : <the exact command>`. **A timed-out reviewer is RESUMED,
 223:   not re-asked from scratch** - run that command as printed (`-Mode resume -Thread <id>
 224:   ... -Prompt "finish your review"`; it carries the run's own options - timeout, effort, word
 225:   cap, schema transport, config, artifacts, range); it keeps everything the reviewer read.
 226:   Read the partial file before deciding anything on it: it is unfinished work, not a verdict.
 227: - `-Artifact <path>` â€” hash a built artifact (an executable, a bundle) into the ledger
 228:   so the review is bound to it, not just to the source tree. Several paths go in ONE
 229:   comma-separated string (`-Artifact a.exe,b.dll`); the parameter cannot be repeated
 230:   (PowerShell refuses a parameter given twice). A missing path refuses the run
 231:   rather than silently skipping the binding.
 232: - `-Raw` â€” 0.1-style plain-text reply: no structured schema, no findings bookkeeping.
 233:   Use it for a quick informal ask that is not going into the findings ledger.
 234: - `-Panel` (`-PanelAll`: every eligible roster entry, `"weighty"` ones included whatever the
 235:   purpose) â€” send the **same brief to as many roster reviewers as the purpose needs**
 236:   (0.5.0: chore, none and checkpoint 1, diff-review 2, framing and decision 3, core-contract
 237:   and acceptance 4, stuck every eligible one; `-PanelSize <n>` to choose), seated by their
 238:   track record (`-PanelOrder routed`, the default; `roster` keeps the roster order), in
 239:   parallel across endpoints (one after another within one endpoint), each its own
 240:   consultation, own lineage and own reply file. `-PanelConcurrency 1` runs them strictly one
 241:   after another. Needs a reviewer roster; refused with `-Provider`, `-Thread`, or `-Mode
 242:   resume`. See "The panel" below.
 243: - `-Topic a,b` (0.5.0) â€” what the consultation is about (slugs, e.g. `security,tests`): ledger
 244:   `topics[]`, copied onto its rating; a routed panel scores its members on those topics.
 245: - `-Require <reviewer>[,...]` (0.5.0; `-Panel`, or one `-Provider` run) â€” reviewers that must
 246:   take part: `#<roster position>`, a provider label, or `<provider> :: <model>` (with ` [agy]`
 247:   / ` [muse]` for an engine entry). One that is out refuses the run **before anything starts,
 248:   exit 5**, naming who, why and when it is back; a required panel member that fails stops the
 249:   panel (exit 5). A panel takes the roster's `"require"` for its purpose by default; `-Require
 250:   none` drops it - only after the operator agreed to go on without them.
 251: - `-Role <name>` / `-Roles a,b` (0.5.0) â€” give the reviewer (every member) one narrow role, or
 252:   a panel one role per member by score rank: `edge-cases`, `security`, `tests`, `docs` ship
 253:   (`templates/role-<name>.md`); a repository adds its own as `<CollabDir>/roles/<name>.md`.
 254:   The role narrows what the reviewer looks at; the reply format and verdict rules stay.
 255: - `-SchemaTransport output-schema|prompt-only|native` â€” override caps-v1's declared reply-schema
 256:   transport for this one run (not with `-Raw`); use it only when you know the endpoint's
 257:   declared transport is wrong for it right now, not as a routine override.
 258: - `-CollabDir <path>` (default `.collab`), `-CodexExe <path>` if `codex` is not on `PATH`.
 259: - `-DryRun` â€” print the argv, the resolved paths and the planned ledger entry without
 260:   calling Codex. Use it when a call fails and you need to see what would be sent.
 261: - `-Detach` (0.5.0) â€” run the consultation in the background and get your turn back in
 262:   seconds; come back with `-Status -Id <id8>` / `-Wait -Id <id8>`. See "Parking a
 263:   consultation" below.
 264: 
 265: The script creates `handoffs/` and `sessions.json` when missing, and writes (with the
 266: `agy` or `muse` engine the prefix is `agy` / `muse` instead of `codex`, and a denial-retry or format-repair
 267: turn keeps its own `.denial-retry.events.jsonl` / `.repair.events.jsonl` next to them):
 268: 
 269: - `handoffs/<NN>-codex-<slug>.md` â€” header, the verbatim reply, and (unless `-Raw`)
 270:   the rendered findings/verdict/blockers/unproven/first-run-checklist sections;
 271: - `handoffs/<NN>-codex-<slug>.reply.json` â€” the raw structured reply, byte for byte
 272:   (structured mode only);
 273: - `handoffs/<NN>-codex-<slug>.events.jsonl` â€” the raw event stream;
 274: - `handoffs/<NN>-codex-<slug>.original.md` â€” the first-turn prose, only after a format
 275:   repair (see step 3);
 276: - `findings.json` â€” every finding from this reply, appended (structured mode only,
 277:   only when there is at least one finding);
 278: - `sessions.json` â€” one ledger entry appended, the commit point for this consult.
 279: 
 280: A launched run that fails exits non-zero and is still recorded as an entry, so the ledger
 281: is a complete history and not just a success log. A refusal (bad arguments, an unusable
 282: roster, a preflight refusal, a live previous run, `-OffPeakOnly`) exits non-zero with a
 283: `codex-consult: <message>` line and writes nothing.
 284: 
 285: ## 3. Read, verify, record
 286: 
 287: Read the reply file. **Verify every finding yourself** before acting on it â€” open the
 288: cited location, run the build, run the test. Codex proposes; you verify and decide.
 289: A reviewer may answer in plain prose instead of the requested JSON object (most often on
 290: a route that does not enforce the schema: z.ai, or a `prompt-only` route such as MiMo).
 291: With `-FormatRetry 1` (the default) the bridge then spends ONE recorded repair turn on
 292: the same thread when the prose is substantive (in the run's own schema transport - ledger
 293: `format_retry.schema_transport`); when the repair was not attempted
 294: (`format_retry` is `null` and `validation_error` says why) or failed, the prose is kept
 295: with no verdict and no findings, which is not a bridge failure. Only then re-ask once,
 296: explicitly asking it to "return the JSON object", if you need this consultation's
 297: findings tracked.
 298: 
 299: When `format_retry.succeeded` is `true` in the ledger entry, the ingested findings and
 300: verdict came from a repair turn that converted a prose reply after the fact â€” **read the
 301: drift notes (`format_retry.drift[]`) before trusting them**. If a drift note disagrees
 302: with what the structured reply says (a different verdict, a numbered answer that does
 303: not match, a finding named in the prose but missing from the object), the original prose
 304: â€” kept byte for byte as `handoffs/NN-codex-<slug>.original.md` â€” is the evidence of
 305: record, not the repaired object.
 306: 
 307: If the reply ends with a `## Requested checks` section (`RC1..RCn`, at most 5 â€” a
 308: convention, not a schema field), run each one yourself or hand it to a worker,
 309: then fill the `## Requested checks run` table in the next brief
 310: (`templates/brief-review.md`) with the command, the revision it ran against, its exit
 311: status, where the log or observation lives, and its state
 312: (`completed`/`failed`/`skipped`). Cite that table's rows, not a paraphrase, when the
 313: next brief references what was checked.
 314: 
 315: Then record the outcome with the findings tool, not by paraphrasing it into a summary:
 316: 
 317: ```
 318: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-findings.ps1" -Task <task> -Id F04-1 -Status implemented|verified|rejected|wontfix|superseded -Note "<why>" -Evidence "<what you ran / where the proof is>"
 319: ```
 320: 
 321: `verified` requires `-Evidence` â€” what you ran and what it showed, not just that you
 322: believe it; `rejected` and a reopen (`-Status proposed` on a non-`proposed` finding)
 323: require `-Note`; `superseded` requires neither. A reviewer reporting a finding "fixed"
 324: in a later reply's `prior_findings` is evidence you can cite, never a status change by
 325: itself: the coordinator still moves the status. A **still-open prior blocker** Codex
 326: reports as `still-open` while itself answering `ACCEPT` invalidates that ACCEPT â€” the
 327: script drops the verdict and records the contradiction, so an ACCEPT on a task with a
 328: known open blocker is never quietly taken at face value. `powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-findings.ps1" -Task <task> -Stats` prints effort, wall time, tokens
 329: and finding counts per consultation â€” the R5 measurement of what each review purpose
 330: actually cost and produced.
 331: 
 332: `-Id`/`-Status` holds the same task lock as a running consultation and is **refused**
 333: while one is in progress for that task â€” a whole `-Panel` run included â€” (under the same
 334: live-process rules, without ever modifying a recovery record); its write, like `-Rate`'s,
 335: goes through the task's commit write lock on a freshly re-read `findings.json`. `-List`
 336: (which flags `[ORPHAN]` findings â€” a crash between the findings write and the ledger
 337: write) and `-Stats` only read and never take the lock. `.consult.lock` and
 338: `.consult.write.lock` are permanent and git-ignored â€” deleting them does nothing useful.
 339: `.consult.pending.json` (a panel member's: `.consult.pending-<NN>.json`) means a run in
 340: progress or an interrupted one; the next consultation recovers it automatically unless the
 341: bridge that wrote it or a codex process from it is still alive, in which case it is
 342: refused and the message says which pid.
 343: 
 344: **Rate the consultation.** After recording the findings (or confirming a prose reply
 345: raised none), mark whether it was actually useful:
 346: 
 347: ```
 348: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-findings.ps1" -Task <task> -Rate <n> -Useful yes|partly|no -Note "<why, required for no>"
 349: ```
 350: 
 351: `<n>` is the ledger entry number of that consultation, not a finding id. Rate **every**
 352: consultation, including a plain-prose reply that produced no ids â€” skipping those means
 353: the telemetry only ever counts structured reviewers, which biases the scoreboard toward
 354: whoever happens to answer in JSON. `codex-scoreboard.ps1` (below) sums these marks per
 355: reviewer and purpose, and (0.5.0) a routed `-Panel` seats its members by them - the mark is
 356: keyed by the consultation's id and carries its reviewer, purpose, topics and time, so it counts
 357: across every task of the repository. A **failed** consultation may be rated too: `-Useful no` only when the
 358: failure was the reviewer's (a refusal, an invented finding, a reply it could not put in the
 359: format); **skip the rating** when the bridge's timeout or a plan limit (a usage limit, a
 360: quota) killed it - resume it instead (see "Run one command").
 361: 
 362: ## Role split: the operator's council
 363: 
 364: Treat every reviewer in play â€” Claude (this coordinator), Codex, and any roster member
 365: â€” as a council with these rules, not as a primary reviewer plus optional extras:
 366: 
 367: - **The coordinator is an equal participant, not a rubber stamp**, and is the judge by
 368:   default: its own ideas are on the table alongside every reviewer's. For a genuinely
 369:   hard question, the judge role can be handed to one reviewer explicitly â€” a
 370:   `-Purpose decision` consultation whose brief references the other members' reply
 371:   files by path and asks for a verdict; record that verdict in `state.md` as the
 372:   decision, but the coordinator still executes and verifies it.
 373: - **Every brief goes to the panel by default (`-Panel`)**, sized by its stakes (0.5.0: the
 374:   purpose's size - 1 for a checkpoint or a chore, 2 for a diff review, 3 for framing and
 375:   decisions, 4 for core contracts and acceptance, every eligible reviewer when stuck). Cheap
 376:   roster members join every brief; weighty ones (roster `"panel": "weighty"`) join only the
 377:   weighty purposes (`framing`, `decision`, `core-contract`, `acceptance`, `stuck`) unless you
 378:   pass `-PanelAll`. Tokens are finite for every provider â€” do not spend a weighty
 379:   reviewer on a checkpoint or a routine diff review unless the question is hard.
 380: - **Framing and decision questions go to a panel of at least one companion - never only your
 381:   own judgement** (the design floor): a framing or decision panel that seats fewer than 2
 382:   members warns (`panel floor: ...`, console and ledger `warnings[]`) - add a reviewer, or say
 383:   in `state.md` why one reviewer is enough (then pass `-PanelSize 1`, which silences it). Past
 384:   about five diverse members findings tend to repeat - an operational heuristic, measured by
 385:   the scoreboard's `UNIQ` column, not a rule.
 386: - **Rate every consultation (`codex-findings.ps1 -Rate`)**: a routed panel seats its members by
 387:   those marks (every task of the repository, the last 90 days); without 3 marks for any
 388:   eligible reviewer it keeps the roster order. Give a question its `-Topic` so the marks can
 389:   be told apart by topic later.
 390: - **A provider without a credential or without tokens left is simply not used** â€” the
 391:   roster skips it and records why (see the README's "Reviewer roster and panel"); a fallback reviewer's
 392:   reply is never presented as the primary's, and lineage stays per reviewer â€” no
 393:   fork/resume across providers, panel or not.
 394: - **Disagreement is the signal, not noise.** Record it in `state.md` as an open item
 395:   until evidence settles who was right; `codex-findings.ps1 -Stats`'s per-reviewer
 396:   scoreboard shows, over time, who actually finds what.
 397: - **Before picking a panel or a judge for a hard question, check the scoreboard.** Run
 398:   `codex-scoreboard.ps1` (see the README's "Usefulness telemetry: codex-scoreboard.ps1") to see which
 399:   reviewer has actually been useful on that purpose so far, not just who is cheapest or
 400:   fastest (0.5.0: its `SCORE` column is the score a routed panel uses; `-By topic` shows the
 401:   rows per topic).
 402: - **Chores go to cheap members.** Hand bounded search/extraction work to a cheap roster
 403:   member with `-Purpose chore`, and pre-digest large inputs before a weighty brief â€” put
 404:   the extract in the brief, not the raw file.
 405: - **Acceptance authority for a release stays with the reviewer who raised the
 406:   findings.** A stand-in's ACCEPT is recorded, but the tag waits for the one who raised
 407:   them.
 408: 
 409: When a fresh-context verifier of the same model family (Claude, in the mechanics role)
 410: is also reviewing, that split is a further, orthogonal division of labor, not exclusive
 411: responsibilities â€” either may challenge anything the other says:
 412: 
 413: - **The verifier** is best used for mechanics: lint, interpreter/version compatibility,
 414:   build correctness, test wiring, whether the code does what a summary claims it does.
 415: - **Codex** is best used for protocol and state-machine correctness, and for naming
 416:   what the evidence does not show â€” the failure modes a mechanical read does not surface.
 417: 
 418: On a real multi-wave task the two typically find mostly different defects; treat both
 419: as required coverage, not as a redundant second look.
 420: 
 421: ## The panel
 422: 
 423: `-Panel` (a reviewer roster is required â€” see the README's "Reviewer roster and panel") sends the **same
 424: brief to the roster entries it seats**: each member is a complete, independent
 425: consultation â€” its own preflight, its own lineage, its own reply file
 426: (`handoffs/NN-codex-<ReplyName>-<provider>.md`) and its own ledger entry (`panel`
 427: field). `-PanelAll` includes `"weighty"` roster entries whatever the purpose; without
 428: it, a `"weighty"` entry only joins on the weighty purposes.
 429: 
 430: - **Size and seats (0.5.0; the README's "Companions")** â€” the panel starts as many members as
 431:   the purpose needs (`-PanelSize` overrides; no backfill for a member that fails); an eligible
 432:   entry without a seat is `not picked: panel size k`, never a skip. The seats are drawn by the
 433:   routing scores with a lab-diversity reserve and 20 % exploration - a seeded, reproducible
 434:   draw: a dry run and the real run of the same day seat the same members (`-PanelSeed` pins
 435:   the nonce) - or, while no eligible reviewer has 3 marks, the roster order. The first lines
 436:   print `Routing: ...` (the eligible entries with their lab and score, the seats and the rule
 437:   that filled each); every member's ledger `panel.routing` records the same, and the summary
 438:   says `asked k, started j, usable i`.
 439: - **Required reviewers** (`-Require`, the roster's `"require"`) take their seats first; one
 440:   that is out refuses the panel before anything starts (exit `5`) - see section 0 above.
 441: 
 442: - **Parallel across endpoints** (0.4.x wave 21) â€” members run as processes of their own,
 443:   at once when they reach different endpoints, one after another within one endpoint (one
 444:   provider label, or labels on one provider fingerprint such as all agy labels); the
 445:   roster's top-level `"parallel": {"<label>": n}` raises a label's limit, and
 446:   `-PanelConcurrency <n>` caps the total (`1` = strictly one after another). The panel
 447:   takes about as long as its slowest member, and it holds the task lock for the whole
 448:   panel: no `codex-findings.ps1 -Status`/`-Rate` on that task until it ends. The ledger
 449:   stays sorted by `n` (seat order - `panel.routing.picked`) whatever finishes first.
 450: - A failing member does not stop the rest. With `-PanelConcurrency 1` a member whose
 451:   failure leaves surviving processes stops the remaining members â€” recorded `skipped` with
 452:   reason `not started: the previous member (<lineage>) left surviving processes
 453:   (.consult.pending-<NN>.json state survivors); recover the task first` (F15-3); at the
 454:   default the others run on, and the kept record blocks the task afterwards until it is
 455:   recovered.
 456: - **Do not run other consultations in the repository beside a panel with agy members**:
 457:   an agy member's read-only check fails on any collab change outside its own task's stores
 458:   and its siblings' handoffs.
 459: - **Per-lineage** â€” each member forks the newest thread of its own lineage (or starts
 460:   one); never fork or resume one member's thread under another's provider/model.
 461: - **Members see the same open-findings snapshot** â€” every member is shown the findings
 462:   that were open when the panel started, not a later member's answer. This is **NOT
 463:   blind between waves**: within one panel run, all members see the same pre-panel
 464:   state, but a LATER panel (on the same task) will see findings the earlier panel
 465:   raised, exactly as a normal sequential consultation would.
 466: - A summary block closes the run (one line per member: lineage, verdict or failure,
 467:   finding counts; `(after a timeout continuation)` for a member that answered on its
 468:   continuation turn, `partial <path>` for one whose work was salvaged); the run exits `0`
 469:   only when every member produced a usable reply. Each member continues inside its own
 470:   process after a timeout kill; a member that still failed is resumed on its own (its output
 471:   in the panel's prints the command) - never re-run the whole panel for it.
 472: - Record every member's findings normally with `codex-findings.ps1`; nothing about a
 473:   panel changes the status lifecycle. There is still no `-Link`/`-Stats -Group` tooling
 474:   for corroboration or contradiction between members â€” compare replies by hand and use
 475:   `-Stats`'s scoreboard to see who finds what over time (ROADMAP R9, deferred to 0.4.0).
 476: 
 477: Without `-Panel`, `-Provider` still lets you consult one specific reviewer on the same
 478: wire (e.g. a specific roster member, or any `[model_providers.<name>]` entry) â€” see the
 479: README's "Reviewer identity and lineage" and "Effort vocabularies (caps-v1)" for how
 480: identity, lineage and effort are resolved for a single-reviewer run.
 481: 
 482: ## Parking a consultation (-Detach, 0.5.0)
 483: 
 484: A panel acceptance runs 15-60 minutes. Do not sit in it: add `-Detach` to the command and
 485: carry on with other work.
 486: 
 487: ```
 488: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-consult.ps1" -Task <task> -Panel -Purpose acceptance -TimeoutSec 3600 -Brief .collab/<task>/handoffs/<NN>-claude-<slug>.md -ReplyName <slug> -Detach
 489: ```
 490: 
 491: - **It is checked before it returns.** A refusal (a missing brief, no available reviewer, no
 492:   launcher, a live consultation of the task) comes back at once, exit `1`, nothing written -
 493:   fix it as for a blocking run. Exit `0` prints three lines: `Detached <id8>: ...`, the status
 494:   file, the come-back commands.
 495: - **Park it**: write into the task's `state.md` the detach id (`<id8>`), the brief's path and
 496:   the exact come-back command (`codex-consult.ps1 -Task <task> -Status -Id <id8>`). A later
 497:   session finds it there - and in the SessionStart line (`; 1 detached consultation running
 498:   (task <task>)`) and in `codex-findings.ps1 -Task <task> -List` (`detached <id8>: running
 499:   since ...`).
 500: - **Meanwhile**: never start a second consultation on the same task (the task lock refuses it
 501:   anyway, as it refuses `codex-findings.ps1 -Id/-Status/-Rate`), never edit the brief or the
 502:   files under review (the run is bound to them), and do not act on a reply you have not read.
 503:   Other tasks are free - except beside a panel with agy members: an agy member fails on any
 504:   change elsewhere under the collab directory, a detached one too.
 505: - **Come back after `done`, never before.** `-Status -Id <id8>` never blocks: exit `2` =
 506:   still running (members `running` / `usable` / `failed` so far - a partial picture, not a
 507:   result), `0` = done and every member usable, `1` = done with a failure, or the background
 508:   died (then the next run of the task recovers its records as usual; re-run what is missing).
 509:   Once done it prints the run's summary block - the same lines a blocking run prints; read the
 510:   reply files it names and go on with step 3 as usual.
 511: - **Or wait for it**: `-Wait -Id <id8> -WaitTimeoutSec <s>` with `<s>` below your own tool's
 512:   command timeout (e.g. 540 for a 10-minute limit); exit `3` = still running after `<s>` (the
 513:   run is untouched) - wait again or come back later. Without `-WaitTimeoutSec` it waits up to
 514:   the run's budget (`budget_sec`: its timeouts, retries and continuation, per endpoint group).
 515: - `-Status` without `-Id` shows every detached run of the task (the worst state decides the
 516:   exit code); an id prefix that matches several runs is refused (exit `4`). `-Status -Prune`
 517:   deletes the status files and logs of runs that finished or died more than 7 days ago (0.5.0:
 518:   also an unreadable status file 7 days after its last write; `-Status` prints the command that
 519:   removes a younger one). A background that could not make its status final exits `6`: read
 520:   its log (`.consult.detached-<id8>.log`) - the result is only there.
 521: 
 522: ## Invariants
 523: 
 524: 1. **Read-only by default.** Use `-Sandbox workspace-write` only when the user has
 525:    explicitly made Codex the author of a stage. `danger-full-access` is refused by
 526:    the script and there is no flag to force it.
 527: 2. **Exec options before the subcommand.** `codex exec [options] fork|resume <id>` â€”
 528:    `--sandbox`, `--json`, `-o`, `-m`, `-c` and `--color` placed *after* `fork` fail
 529:    with "unexpected argument". The script already gets this right; keep it that way
 530:    if you edit the command.
 531: 3. **The prompt goes on stdin.** The script pipes it via `-`. A prompt passed as a
 532:    positional argument is re-expanded by the Windows `codex.cmd` shim, which eats
 533:    `%VAR%` patterns.
 534: 4. **Claude keeps the final word.** A consultation is evidence, not an instruction.
 535: 5. **Project isolation.** Everything is scoped to the git repository you run from:
 536:    the ledger lives under `<repo>/<CollabDir>/<task>/`, the parent thread for
 537:    `fork`/`resume` comes only from *that* repository's `sessions.json`, and a
 538:    repository with no ledger starts a fresh thread. Never pass `-Thread <uuid>` taken
 539:    from another project's ledger, and never point a brief at files outside the
 540:    repository â€” the read-only sandbox blocks writes, not reads, so the brief is what
 541:    keeps projects apart.
 542: 6. **One Codex thread belongs to one task directory.** Not enforced by the script â€”
 543:    resuming the same thread from two different task directories is on you to avoid.
 544: 7. **A verdict is not an outcome.** `bridge_outcome` says the bridge worked â€” a reply
 545:    came back and was written to disk. `verdict` says what the reviewer decided. A
 546:    delivered HOLD is a success of the bridge: the run worked exactly as intended.
 547: 8. **Never use a provider without a credential or without tokens left.** The roster
 548:    exists so this is checked automatically, not assumed; a provider `codex-providers.ps1`
 549:    or a roster walk reports skipped/unavailable is not planned on.
 550: 9. **A fallback reviewer's reply is never presented as the primary's.** Lineage stays
 551:    per reviewer; note explicitly which reviewer actually answered, panel or not.
 552: 10. **Judge delegation is explicit.** The coordinator is the judge by default; handing
 553:     that role to one reviewer for a hard question is a deliberate `-Purpose decision`
 554:     consultation referencing the other members' replies, recorded in `state.md` â€” never
 555:     an implicit "whoever answered ACCEPT wins".

   1: ---
   2: name: setup-providers
   3: description: Wire reviewers for the codex-consult bridge on a machine - verify the Codex CLI and its login, add a [model_providers.<name>] table for a third-party plan (z.ai GLM, Xiaomi MiMo or any Responses-API provider) with an env_key the user sets, supply per-run model catalogs, wire Gemini through the agy engine (Google's Antigravity CLI, signed in by the user), wire Meta Muse through the muse engine (Muse Code CLI, the subscription signed in by the user with muse login, never an API key), write the reviewer roster with panel weights, and verify with codex-providers.ps1 and a dry run. Use when a provider is missing or unavailable, on a new machine, or when the user asks to add a reviewer.
   4: argument-hint: "[provider name, e.g. ZAI or mimo]"
   5: allowed-tools: Bash(powershell:*), Bash(pwsh:*), Bash(codex:*), Bash(agy models), Bash(muse --version), Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, WebFetch
   6: disable-model-invocation: false
   7: ---
   8: 
   9: # Set up reviewers for codex-consult
  10: 
  11: This procedure wires one or more reviewers so `codex-consult.ps1` can reach them. A
  12: reviewer goes through `codex exec` (the default engine) or, per roster entry, through
  13: Google's Antigravity CLI `agy` (the `agy` engine, section 3b) or Meta's Muse Code CLI `muse`
  14: (the `muse` engine, section 3f); the bridge itself never makes an HTTP call. Scripts:
  15: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/`. Commands are shown for Windows PowerShell; on macOS/Linux
  16: use `pwsh -NoProfile -File` in place of `powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File`.
  17: `<codex home>` is `$CODEX_HOME` when set, else `~/.codex`.
  18: 
  19: ## Invariants (never break these)
  20: 
  21: 1. **Keys never go into files, output or chat.** You do not create, print, echo, log,
  22:    commit or paste an API key, and you do not read one back from the environment. The
  23:    user sets it; you only check that it is set, through `codex-providers.ps1`.
  24: 2. **One thread = one provider and model.** Never fork or resume a thread under another
  25:    provider or model; the bridge refuses it, and you do not work around it.
  26: 3. **Preflight is fail-closed.** A refusal (`provider X is not usable: â€¦`,
  27:    `availability could not be established`) is information, not an obstacle. Never
  28:    pass `-SkipPreflight` to get past a real refusal.
  29: 4. **The roster never replaces an available primary.** It orders the reviewers the user
  30:    is willing to use; a fallback reviewer's reply is never presented as the primary's.
  31: 5. **Never invent** a base URL, a model name, a region or a peak schedule. Take them from
  32:    the provider's official page or from the user.
  33: 6. **Ask before** installing software, editing `config.toml`, downloading a catalog, or
  34:    running a first live consultation (it spends quota).
  35: 
  36: ## 1. Verify the Codex CLI and the login
  37: 
  38: ```
  39: codex --version                 # expect: codex-cli 0.148 or newer (tested: codex-cli 0.155.1)
  40: codex login status              # expect: Logged in using ChatGPT
  41: ```
  42: 
  43: Missing CLI: ask the user to install it (https://github.com/openai/codex). Not logged in:
  44: ask the user to run `codex login` in their own terminal. The built-in `openai` provider
  45: needs no table. Then check the config's top level without printing the file (it may hold
  46: a token):
  47: 
  48: ```powershell
  49: $cfg = Join-Path $(if ($env:CODEX_HOME) { $env:CODEX_HOME } else { "$HOME/.codex" }) 'config.toml'
  50: Select-String -Path $cfg -Pattern '^\s*(model|model_provider|profile|model_catalog_json)\s*=', '^\s*\['
  51: ```
  52: 
  53: Want: a top-level `model = "â€¦"` (without it, a run with no `-Model` and no roster entry
  54: has an unresolved identity and can only start new threads); no top-level `profile` (it
  55: disables `fork`/`resume` for every run); no top-level `model_catalog_json` (it replaces
  56: Codex's own catalog and degrades unrelated models). Ask the user before changing any of
  57: them.
  58: 
  59: ## 2. Add a provider table
  60: 
  61: Read the provider's official Codex page (WebFetch is fine) and take `base_url` and
  62: `wire_api` from it:
  63: 
  64: - z.ai GLM Coding Plan: https://docs.z.ai/devpack/tool/codex (page shows
  65:   `base_url = "https://api.z.ai/api/v1"`, `wire_api = "responses"`)
  66: - Xiaomi MiMo Token Plan: https://mimo.mi.com/docs/en-US/tokenplan/integration/codex-configuration
  67:   (page shows `https://token-plan-cn.xiaomimimo.com/v1`; the user's plan console names
  68:   their region, e.g. `token-plan-ams`; pay-as-you-go `https://api.xiaomimimo.com/v1`)
  69: 
  70: Both pages put the key into the file as `experimental_bearer_token`. Replace that line with
  71: `env_key`. Shape, appended to `<codex home>/config.toml` after the user agrees:
  72: 
  73: ```toml
  74: [model_providers.ZAI]
  75: name = "Z.ai GLM Coding Plan"
  76: base_url = "https://api.z.ai/api/v1"
  77: env_key = "ZAI_API_KEY"
  78: wire_api = "responses"
  79: ```
  80: 
  81: Conventions:
  82: - The table name is the provider name everywhere (`-Provider ZAI`, roster
  83:   `"provider": "ZAI"`, `CODEX_CONSULT_PEAK_ZAI`); case-sensitive, short, ASCII. The env
  84:   variable is `<NAME>_API_KEY` unless the user already uses another name.
  85: - Plain single-line values only: no arrays, inline tables, multi-line strings, dotted keys
  86:   or sub-tables inside the table (the bridge's scanner then marks the table unusable).
  87: - Always write `wire_api = "responses"` explicitly. Changing `base_url` or `wire_api` later
  88:   starts a new lineage (older threads can no longer be forked); `name`, comments and a
  89:   rotated key never do.
  90: - Only in the user-level `<codex home>/config.toml`: the bridge reads no other Codex
  91:   config, so a table anywhere else is invisible to its identity and preflight.
  92: 
  93: Then tell the user to set the key themselves and restart Claude Code (a running session
  94: does not see a variable set after it started):
  95: 
  96: - Windows: `setx ZAI_API_KEY "<key>"` in their own terminal
  97: - macOS/Linux: `export ZAI_API_KEY="<key>"` in `~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc` or `~/.profile`
  98: 
  99: Never ask them to paste the key into the chat.
 100: 
 101: Models: use one the bridge's caps-v1 table declares for the host (z.ai: `glm-5.3`,
 102: `glm-5.3-flash`, `glm-5.3-flashx`, `glm-5.2`, `glm-5.1`, `glm-5`, `glm-5-turbo`,
 103: `glm-4.7`, `glm-4.6`, `glm-4.5`, `glm-4.5-air`; MiMo: `mimo-v2.6-pro`, `mimo-v2.6-flash`,
 104: `mimo-v2.6-pro-ultraspeed`, `mimo-v2.5-pro`, `mimo-v2.5`). Any other model, or any host
 105: not in caps-v1, needs `-NativeEffort <value>` on every run, which a roster entry cannot
 106: supply.
 107: 
 108: ## 3. Per-run model catalogs (MiMo-style)
 109: 
 110: Codex has no built-in catalog for MiMo models. With the user's consent, save the catalog
 111: file the MiMo Codex page links to as `<codex home>/model-catalogs.json`, and pass it PER
 112: RUN, never in `config.toml`: a global `model_catalog_json` replaces Codex's own catalog
 113: and was observed to degrade the default `openai` model on an unrelated run ("Model
 114: metadata not found, fallback"). Per run means the roster entry's
 115: `"codex_config": ["model_catalog_json=~/.codex/model-catalogs.json"]`, or
 116: `-CodexConfig model_catalog_json=~/.codex/model-catalogs.json` on one command (the bridge
 117: expands `~/`; Codex on Windows does not). The same rule applies to any provider whose page
 118: suggests a global catalog (z.ai's suggests `~/.codex/models.json`; the z.ai route works
 119: without one).
 120: 
 121: ## 3b. Gemini through the agy engine (Google's Antigravity CLI)
 122: 
 123: For the Gemini models under a Google AI Pro plan, the reviewer is reached through `agy`, the
 124: official headless client (the plan terms allow only the official clients; no
 125: `GEMINI_API_KEY` mode). It enforces the reply schema natively (`--json-schema`).
 126: 
 127: 1. **Install** (ask the user): `winget install Google.AntigravityCLI`, or the official
 128:    installer (it puts `agy.exe` under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\agy\bin`). Check:
 129:    `(Get-Command agy.exe).Source` -> a path. Not on PATH: the user passes `-EngineExe
 130:    <path>` or sets `CODEX_CONSULT_AGY_EXE`.
 131: 2. **Sign in - the USER does it:** they run `agy` once in their own terminal and sign in
 132:    with their Google account (the credentials go to the OS keyring). You never handle a
 133:    login, a token or a keyring entry.
 134: 3. **Check:** `agy models` -> exit `0` and lines `<model id><TAB><name>`, e.g.
 135:    `gemini-3.8-flash-high  Gemini 3.8 Flash (High)`. The model id is the FULL id; its last
 136:    part is the reasoning tier (`-high`, `-medium`, `-low`) - the bridge sends no effort for
 137:    agy. Take the model ids from this list; never invent one.
 138: 4. **Roster entries** (section 4): `{ "provider": "gemini", "engine": "agy", "model":
 139:    "gemini-3.8-flash-high" }` - `provider` is a free label (the lineage's provider), the
 140:    model is required, `codex_config` and `auth` are refused, one label names one engine
 141:    across the roster. For weighty asks add a second entry with the same label on the pro
 142:    model, `{ "provider": "gemini", "engine": "agy", "model": "gemini-3.1-pro-high",
 143:    "panel": "weighty" }`; a single run picks it with `-Provider gemini -Model
 144:    gemini-3.1-pro-high`.
 145: 5. **Cost:** every agy call carries about 13-25k tokens of the CLI's own prompt and tools,
 146:    and a resumed conversation replays itself (the bridge defaults agy to `-Mode new`); a diff
 147:    review on `gemini-3.8-flash-high` reads the tree (observed: 605 s, 1.6M input + 5.9M
 148:    cached tokens). Google AI Pro refreshes the quota every five hours until a weekly limit;
 149:    the CLI cannot show the remaining quota; the bridge records `usage` per run.
 150: 6. **Read-only is not enforced by agy** (its `--sandbox` restricts the terminal only): the
 151:    bridge fails an agy run when the working tree (tracked or untracked files) or the collab
 152:    directory (every task's stores and handoffs) changed during it - enforced by evidence for
 153:    tracked and untracked files and the collab directory; not for gitignored paths,
 154:    submodules or files outside the repository. The check cannot tell who changed a file:
 155:    tell the user not to edit the repository or the collab directory, and not to run another
 156:    consultation in that repository, while an agy consultation runs.
 157: 7. **Sign-in timing:** `agy models` usually answers in ~2 s but has taken 15 s and more; the
 158:    bridge waits up to 45 s, and skips the call when the repository's ledgers hold a usable
 159:    agy reply from the last 60 minutes (`ok: signed in (usable reply <m> min ago)`).

 161: ## 3c. BytePlus ModelArk Coding Plan (a Codex provider)
 162: 
 163: The international ModelArk Coding Plan (BytePlus, region ap-southeast-1; Lite 10 USD / month)
 164: bundles Dola-Seed (Doubao), GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi and gpt-oss behind one subscription quota
 165: and speaks the Responses API on its Codex base URL, so it is an ordinary provider table:
 166: 
 167: ```toml
 168: [model_providers.byteplus]
 169: name = "BytePlus ModelArk Coding Plan (ap-southeast-1)"
 170: base_url = "https://ark.ap-southeast.bytepluses.com/api/coding/v3"
 171: env_key = "BYTEPLUS_API_KEY"

 173: ```

 176:   and does not touch the plan quota. The plan's own rule: its key and base URL are for the
 177:   supported coding tools (Codex CLI is one) - other uses may be treated as abuse.
 178: - The user creates the API key in the ModelArk console ("API keys") and sets the variable
 179:   themselves (`setx BYTEPLUS_API_KEY <value>`, then a NEW terminal). You never handle it.
 180: - caps-v1 declares this host: vocabulary `low | medium | high` (`xhigh` -> `high`, mapping

 185:   `-NativeEffort` is passed. The plan's docs enable reasoning with the Codex option
 186:   `model_supports_reasoning_summaries = true`: pass it per entry as `"codex_config":
 187:   ["model_supports_reasoning_summaries=true"]` (some Kimi code models reject it - check the

 191:   times that. One quota for every model and tool. No refunds; the subscription authorises
 192:   the vendor to use inputs and outputs for training.
 193: - Roster entries are ordinary codex entries: `{ "provider": "byteplus", "model": "kimi-k2.5",
 194:   "codex_config": ["model_supports_reasoning_summaries=true"] }`; the same label may carry
 195:   several models (one entry per model), each a lineage of its own.

 197: ## 3d. Kimi Code membership (Moonshot; a Codex provider)
 198: 
 199: A Kimi membership (Plus and above) includes Kimi Code, whose overseas Codex base URL speaks the
 200: Responses API, so K3 is an ordinary provider table:
 201: 
 202: ```toml
 203: [model_providers.kimi]
 204: name = "Kimi Code membership (Moonshot, overseas)"
 205: base_url = "https://api.kimi.ai/coding/v1"
 206: env_key = "KIMI_API_KEY"

 226: ## 3e. Alibaba Cloud Model Studio Token Plan (Qwen; a Codex provider)
 227: 
 228: The Token Plan (Personal Edition; the Singapore region only) is a monthly credit subscription
 229: whose Codex base URL speaks the Responses API - Qwen 3.8 is sold by subscription only here:

 241:   and sets `ALIBABA_API_KEY` themselves. Two credentials that do NOT belong here: an AccessKey
 242:   ID/Secret pair (cloud-management credentials for the whole account - never put one into a
 243:   coding tool) and a general Model Studio key `sk-...` (it bills pay-as-you-go even while the
 244:   plan is active). Alibaba's own guide puts the key into `OPENAI_API_KEY`; do not - it would

 257:   344k - the two together about 1.7% of the Lite month. The same checkpoint on

 262: - Codex logs "Model metadata for `qwen3.8-max` not found. Defaulting to fallback metadata" -
 263:   harmless in the runs so far.
 264: - Roster entry: `{ "provider": "alibaba", "model": "qwen3.8-max", "panel": "weighty" }`.
 265: 
 266: ## 3f. Meta Muse through the muse engine (Muse Code CLI, the subscription)
 267: 
 268: The Muse Code subscription (the Everyday plan: 10-50 prompts per 5 hours; every muse turn of a
 269: consultation is one prompt) works only through Meta's own CLI signed in by browser. An API
 270: key (`META_API_KEY`, `MODEL_API_KEY`) overrides that sign-in and bills per token - the bridge
 271: therefore REFUSES a muse run while either variable is set, and there is no opt-out.
 272: 
 273: 1. **Install** (ask the user): the official Muse Code installer. On Windows it puts `muse.cmd`
 274:    (a launcher for the versioned binary, which it may update) into
 275:    `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\muse` and adds that directory to the USER Path - a shell (and a
 276:    Claude Code session) started before the install does not see it; the bridge falls back to
 277:    that location by itself. Check without spending a prompt: `muse --version` -> a version
 278:    line (or `Test-Path "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\muse\muse.cmd"` -> `True`). Elsewhere: the
 279:    user passes `-EngineExe <path>` or sets `CODEX_CONSULT_MUSE_EXE`.
 280: 2. **Credential backend - the USER sets it BEFORE signing in, on every OS:** the keychain
 281:    write fails on Windows and the bridge cannot read a keychain anywhere, so the credential must
 282:    go to a file: the user variable `TBH_CREDENTIAL_BACKEND=file` (e.g. `[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('TBH_CREDENTIAL_BACKEND', 'file', 'User')`,
 283:    then a new shell / a restarted Claude Code). Without a readable oauth sign-in the bridge
 284:    REFUSES every muse launch (`the muse engine is refused: the Muse sign-in is not established
 285:    as oauth (TBH_CREDENTIAL_BACKEND is not set: the keychain backend cannot be read): ...`) -
 286:    `-SkipPreflight` does not change that.
 287: 3. **Sign in - the USER does it:** `muse login` in their own terminal shows a device code they
 288:    approve in the browser. The credential then lives in `~/.config/muse/auth.json`. You never
 289:    read, print or copy that file, and never handle a login, a token or a device code.
 290: 4. **Never an API key.** Confirm with the user that neither `META_API_KEY` nor `MODEL_API_KEY`
 291:    is set (ask; do not print the environment). If one is, the user removes it - it would bill
 292:    per token, and the bridge refuses every muse run meanwhile (`the muse engine is refused:
 293:    META_API_KEY is set: ...`, also under `-SkipPreflight`).
 294: 5. **The model - the USER decides:** caps-v1 declares the two subscription models verified
 295:    live: `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` (the CLI's default; Meta may train on its inputs) and
 296:    `muse-spark-1.3` (the standard one). Ask which one; never pick the contributor variant
 297:    silently. The effort goes as `--reasoning-effort` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` as is,
 298:    mapping `muse-v1`).
 299: 6. **Roster entry** (section 4): `{ "provider": "meta", "engine": "muse", "model":
 300:    "muse-spark-1.3" }` - `provider` is a free label, the model is required, `codex_config`
 301:    and `auth` are refused. Every muse entry shares one endpoint (one Meta sign-in): a usage
 302:    limit hit by one blocks them all until its reset.
 303: 7. **Check:** `codex-providers.ps1` -> the row `available  meta  <n>  engine muse  muse
 304:    (<launcher>)  ok: signed in (~/.config/muse/auth.json: providers.meta, mechanism oauth)
 305:    muse (2 declared models)  -`. Other verdicts: `unavailable (refused: the Muse sign-in is
 306:    not established as oauth (~/.config/muse/auth.json does not exist): ...)` (step 3 missing:
 307:    the user runs `muse login`), `unavailable (refused: the Muse sign-in is not established as
 308:    oauth (TBH_CREDENTIAL_BACKEND is not set: ...): ...)` (step 2 missing) - the CREDENTIALS
 309:    column then reads `missing: not signed in: ...` or `unknown: sign-in not checkable: ...` -,
 310:    `unavailable (refused: META_API_KEY is set: ...)` (step 4), `unavailable (muse CLI not found
 311:    on PATH)` (step 1).
 312: 8. **Read-only:** muse runs with `--disable-write --disable-shell --disable-web-tools
 313:    --approval-mode never`, and the bridge fails a muse run when the working tree or the
 314:    collab directory changed during it (by evidence; gitignored paths, submodules, files
 315:    outside the repository and reads - its `read_file` is not confined to the repository - are
 316:    not covered). Tell the user not to edit the repository or run another consultation there
 317:    while a muse consultation runs.
 318: 
 319: ## 4. Write the roster
 320: 
 321: `<codex home>/codex-consult-roster.json`, first choice first:
 322: 
 323: ```json
 324: {
 325:   "roster_version": 1,
 326:   "reviewers": [
 327:     { "provider": "openai", "model": "<the ChatGPT-plan model>", "panel": "weighty" },
 328:     { "provider": "ZAI", "model": "glm-5.3" },
 329:     {
 330:       "provider": "mimo",
 331:       "model": "mimo-v2.6-pro",
 332:       "codex_config": ["model_catalog_json=~/.codex/model-catalogs.json"]
 333:     },
 334:     { "provider": "gemini", "engine": "agy", "model": "gemini-3.8-flash-high" },
 335:     { "provider": "gemini", "engine": "agy", "model": "gemini-3.1-pro-high", "panel": "weighty" },
 336:     { "provider": "meta", "engine": "muse", "model": "muse-spark-1.3" }
 337:   ]
 338: }
 339: ```
 340: 
 341: - Allowed keys only: `roster_version` (must be `1`), `reviewers[]` with `provider`
 342:   (required), `model`, `codex_config` (array of `key=value` strings), `auth`, `panel`,
 343:   `engine` (`codex`, the default, `agy` or `muse`), `lab`, `roles`, `ext`, the optional
 344:   top-level `require` and `ext` (below), and the optional top-level `parallel`
 345:   (`{"<provider label>": n}`, n >= 1: how many `-Panel` members of that label may run at
 346:   once; the default is one at a time per endpoint). An unknown key, an unknown engine, an
 347:   agy or muse entry without a model or with `codex_config`/`auth`, one label with two engines, a
 348:   duplicate `(provider, model)`, a `parallel` value that is not an integer >= 1 or names a
 349:   label the roster does not use, or invalid JSON refuses EVERY run.
 350: - `"panel": "weighty"` for the expensive reviewer: it joins a `-Panel` run only on
 351:   `framing`, `decision`, `core-contract`, `acceptance` and `stuck` (or `-PanelAll`). The
 352:   default is `"always"`.
 353: - (0.5.0, companions) optional per entry: `"lab"` - the lab behind the model for a panel's lab
 354:   diversity (e.g. `"moonshot"`; omitted, the bridge takes the vendor of the model id's prefix -
 355:   qwen alibaba, deepseek, kimi/k3 moonshot, glm zhipu, dola/seed bytedance, mimo xiaomi, gemini
 356:   google, muse meta, gpt openai - never the provider label; set it for a model id outside that
 357:   table, or a routed panel warns); `"roles": ["security", ...]` - the roles the entry is willing
 358:   to take under `-Roles`. Optional top level: `"require": {"acceptance": ["#1"], ...}` - the
 359:   reviewers a panel of that purpose must include (`#<position>`, a label, or `<provider> ::
 360:   <model>` with ` [agy]`/` [muse]` for an engine entry; each must name an entry, else the roster
 361:   is refused); while one is out such a panel is refused with exit 5. `"ext"` (top level and per
 362:   entry) is an object reserved for other implementations that share the file; the bridge
 363:   validates it as an object and ignores it. `roster_version` stays `1`.
 364: - `codex_config` must not set `model`, `model_provider`, `model_reasoning_effort`,
 365:   `profile` or `model_providers.*` (refused).
 366: - Another file: the user sets `CODEX_CONSULT_ROSTER=<path>` (it must exist).
 367:   `CODEX_CONSULT_ROSTER=none` disables the roster.
 368: 
 369: ## 5. Verify
 370: 
 371: ```
 372: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-providers.ps1"
 373: ```
 374: 
 375: Expect exit `0`, a first line `codex config: <path>`, then `endpoint health: <repo>\.collab (<k>
 376: task ledgers, <m> consultations), read at <time> - the ledgers of THIS repository` (usage limits
 377: and auth failures come from the repository you run in), one row per provider, and for each
 378: wired one `available` with `ok: Logged in using ChatGPT` or `ok: env <NAME> set`, e.g.
 379: `available  ZAI  2  custom  https://api.z.ai/api/v1  ok: env ZAI_API_KEY set  zai (11 declared models)  -`,
 380: then `roster: <path> -> would select <provider> :: <model>` and `availability: all <n> reviewers
 381: available` (the SessionStart line; `codex-providers.ps1 -Short` prints it alone). Other
 382: verdicts - the roster walk's own: `unavailable (missing: env <NAME> not set)` (not set, or
 383: Claude Code not restarted), `unavailable (usage limit until <iso>)`, `unavailable (usage limit
 384: hit <iso>, reset unknown; retry after <iso>)` (a limit without a reset time, for 60 minutes;
 385: `burst limit (429) hit ...` - a 429 that names no usage window or quota - for 10, wave 24c),
 386: `unknown (<reason>)` (login check failed, or the config cannot be scanned). An agy roster label gets its own row: `available  gemini  4,5
 387: engine agy  agy (<launcher>)  ok: signed in (N models)  agy (tier in the model id)  -`
 388: (this listing makes one `agy models` call - none, and `ok: signed in (usable reply <m> min
 389: ago)`, after a usable agy reply in this repository within the last 60 minutes; with
 390: `-NoNetwork` the row otherwise reads `not checked (launcher present; run
 391: codex-providers.ps1)` / `unknown (sign-in not checked)` - the SessionStart line counts such an
 392: entry as `not checked`); `unavailable (agy CLI not found on PATH)` or
 393: `unavailable (missing: ``agy models``: <sign-in message>)` otherwise. A muse label's row: see
 394: section 3f, step 7 (its sign-in check is local, so it runs with `-NoNetwork` too). Exit `1` means an
 395: unusable roster, or a `CODEX_CONSULT_ROSTER` file that does not exist; the message names
 396: it.
 397: Per provider: `-Provider <name>` (exit `0` available, `2` unavailable, `3` unknown, `1`
 398: no such provider).
 399: 
 400: Then a dry run inside a git repository, once per reviewer:
 401: 
 402: ```
 403: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/codex-consult.ps1" -Task setup-check -Prompt "Reply with one sentence." -DryRun -Provider ZAI -Model glm-5.3
 404: ```
 405: 
 406: Expect exit `0`, `DRY RUN - nothing was executed and no file was written.`,
 407: `preflight   : available (ok: env ZAI_API_KEY set)`,
 408: `effort      : high sent (requested high, mapping zai-v1, â€¦)`, and a `transport   :`
 409: line (`output-schema` for openai and z.ai, `prompt-only` for MiMo). For agy:
 410: `-DryRun -Engine agy -Provider gemini -Model gemini-3.8-flash-high` -> `engine      : agy -
 411: Gemini (agy) (from -Engine)`, `preflight   : available (ok: signed in (N models))`,
 412: `effort      : nothing sent (requested high, mapping model-tier, ...)`, `transport   :
 413: native (...)` and a `command     : agy -p= --input-format stream-json --output-format
 414: stream-json --model gemini-3.8-flash-high --json-schema <schema> --print-timeout 0 --sandbox
 415: --disable-slash-commands` line. For muse: `-DryRun -Engine muse -Model muse-spark-1.3` ->
 416: `engine      : muse - Meta Muse (muse) (from -Engine)`, `preflight   : available (ok: signed
 417: in (~/.config/muse/auth.json: providers.meta, mechanism oauth))`, `effort      : high sent
 418: (requested high, mapping muse-v1, ...)`, `transport   : native (...): passed as
 419: --output-schema ...` and a `command     : muse exec --json --prompt-file <temp file>
 420: --output-schema <schema> --model muse-spark-1.3 --reasoning-effort high
 421: --no-foreign-personal-context --disable-web-tools --disable-write --disable-shell
 422: --approval-mode never` line (the dry run runs `muse --version` at most, which spends no
 423: prompt; without an oauth sign-in the dry run itself is refused - `the muse engine is refused:
 424: the Muse sign-in is not established as oauth (...)` - fix steps 2 and 3 first). Only with the
 425: user's
 426: consent, run one live `-Purpose chore` consultation to confirm the route end to end
 427: (expect `codex-consult: usable reply - <provider> :: <model>, â€¦`).
 428: 
 429: ## 6. Optional
 430: 
 431: - **Peak windows:** the user sets `CODEX_CONSULT_PEAK_<PROVIDER>="Mon-Fri 14:00-18:00 +08:00"`
 432:   (days, start-end, fixed offset; schedule from the plan's own page) and optionally
 433:   `CODEX_CONSULT_PEAK_<PROVIDER>_EXCEPT="2026-10-01..2026-10-07"`. A run at peak warns;
 434:   `-OffPeakOnly` refuses at peak and when no schedule is set.
 435: - **`-SchemaTransport output-schema|prompt-only`:** a one-run override of caps-v1's
 436:   declared transport, only when you know the declared one is wrong for that endpoint.
 437: - **`"auth": "none"`** in a roster entry: only for a table with neither `env_key` nor a
 438:   bearer token (e.g. a local endpoint); it has no effect on a table that names an
 439:   `env_key`. Such a host is not in caps-v1, so it also needs `-NativeEffort`.
 440: 
 441: ## 7. Record it
 442: 
 443: In the project's `state.md` (or its notes file): the providers wired and their models, the
 444: roster path, order and panel weights, the env variable NAMES (never values), any peak
 445: variables, the `codex-providers.ps1` verdict per provider with the date, and what is still
 446: unavailable and why (and what the user was asked to do about it).

1: <#
   2: .SYNOPSIS
   3:     SessionStart hook: one line saying which reviewers are out right now, and until when.
   4: 
   5: .DESCRIPTION
   6:     Runs at the start of a Claude Code session in any project where the plugin is
   7:     enabled (hooks/hooks.json). Prints ONE line to stdout, which Claude Code adds to the
   8:     agent's context (wave 24, D14-D17 - the line `codex-providers.ps1 -Short` prints):
   9: 
  10:         codex-consult: out - openai :: gpt-6-astra (until Sun 20:35, in 2d 10h), gemini :: *
  11:         (until Sun 21:30, in 2d 11h); 9 of 11 reviewers available
  12: 
  13:     or `codex-consult: all 11 reviewers available`. Every roster entry is judged with the
  14:     roster walk's own verdict (Select-PanelMembers -All: credentials, the launch invariant,
  15:     the endpoint health of THIS repository's ledgers - an auth failure, a usage limit with a
  16:     reset ahead, one without a reset for 60 minutes after it was hit, a burst 429 for 10); the entries of one
  17:     endpoint group that share the state collapse to `<label> :: *`; reset times are LOCAL
  18:     with a rounded relative hint; nothing is cut. An entry whose check needs the network (the
  19:     agy engine's `agy models`) is `not checked` here - "..., 2 not checked" in the count -
  20:     unless THIS repository's ledgers hold a usable reply on that endpoint from the last 60
  21:     minutes (then it is available); a recorded auth failure or usage limit still shows it
  22:     out. The muse engine's sign-in check reads ~/.config/muse/auth.json locally and runs here
  23:     too, as does its billing guard (`meta :: <model> (refused: META_API_KEY is set)`).
  24:     Without a roster: the providers of the Codex config ("... (no reviewer roster)").
  25: 
  26:     When the Codex CLI is not on PATH: `codex-consult: codex CLI not found on PATH - follow
  27:     the setup-providers skill`. Everything else (an unreadable config, an unusable roster, a
  28:     crash inside the check) is reported in the same one-line form and never fails the
  29:     session: the exit code is always 0. No network call, no lock, nothing written: it runs
  30:     `codex-providers.ps1 -Short -Json -NoNetwork` and prints the `line` of its object.
  31: 
  32:     (wave 25, R12) The detached consultations of the repository (codex-consult.ps1 -Detach) add
  33:     one phrase to that line - `; 1 detached consultation running (task t)`, `; 2 detached
  34:     consultations finished (tasks t, u)` (finished in the last 24 h), `; detached consultations:
  35:     1 running (task t), 1 died (task u)` - read from the status files
  36:     <CollabDir>/*/.consult.detached-*.status.json, a background's liveness judged by its pid and
  37:     start time (Get-DetachedPhrase). Nothing when there is none.
  38: 
  39:     Cost: about one second (one `codex login status` for the built-in openai; wave 24b: each
  40:     roster entry's identity and each endpoint's health are resolved once per listing - the
  41:     walk, the availability line and the rows share them - and the ledgers are read once), once
  42:     per session. Disable the hook by disabling the plugin's hooks in Claude Code settings.
  43: 
  44:     Runs on Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7.
  45: #>
  46: [CmdletBinding()]
  47: param(
  48:     # Where consultations are stored (endpoint health is read from every task ledger
  49:     # under it). Relative paths resolve against the git repo root of the current directory.
  50:     [string]$CollabDir = '.collab'
  51: )
  52: 
  53: $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
  54: $line = ''
  55: try {
  56:     $providers = Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'codex-providers.ps1'
  57:     $psExe = (Get-Process -Id $PID).Path
  58:     $codex = Get-Command codex -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
  59:     if (-not $codex) {
  60:         $line = 'codex-consult: codex CLI not found on PATH - follow the setup-providers skill before consulting a reviewer'
  61:     } else {
  62:         $previous = $ErrorActionPreference
  63:         $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
  64:         $raw = @(& $psExe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $providers -Short -Json -NoNetwork -CollabDir $CollabDir 2>&1 | ForEach-Object { "$_" })
  65:         $code = $LASTEXITCODE

{"schema_version":"1","verdict":"ADVISE","verdict_reason":"The design is promising but conflates runtime packaging, identity semantics, and host-specific orchestration, so it needs reframing before implementation.","reply_markdown":"## Framing
R13 bundles four separable concerns: runtime contract, installation/discovery, coordinator identity, and R19 coordination policy. Unlisted options are: (a) a versioned full-payload install containing `scripts/`, `schemas/`, `templates/`, and skills; (b) an AGENTS-only degraded mode against an existing payload root; (c) a host-capability profile mapping policy concepts to each host's primitives. To choose I need Codex's skill loading/indexing cost, whether copied skills may depend on sibling payload, whether agent files support stable model aliases, and whether “same model” means model family or the same endpoint/account.

## Q1
Neither option as stated. Copying only two `SKILL.md` files is not self-contained: the skills reference `scripts/`, `schemas/`, and `templates/`, while the documented fallback `<skill dir>/../..` resolves to `~/.codex` after copying. AGENTS-only is an acceptable minimum only when the runtime payload already exists at an explicit root. Prefer a full-payload install plus thin skill entries; otherwise document AGENTS-only as degraded usage.

## Q2
I found no Claude-dependent behavior in the bridge scripts: they invoke `codex`, resolve paths from `$PSScriptRoot`, and write repository-local stores. The remaining assumptions are textual, such as `codex-consult.ps1` saying “from Claude Code”, and `codex-consult-hook.ps1` assuming Claude Code injects its stdout. Make the hook an optional Claude adapter and neutralize script help.

## Q3
Keep the explicit `CODEX_CONSULT_COORDINATOR` value authoritative. Environment markers identify a host product, not a model, and nested hosts can expose several markers at once. Inference may fill a missing value but must record provenance and never override the explicit value. Also define the comparison tuple: provider, normalized model alias, engine, and endpoint/account are needed before “lineage equals” is meaningful.

## Q4
Use one separate `coordinate` skill plus a small always-on AGENTS rule pointing to it. A section inside `consult-codex` is read mainly when consulting, missing delegation-only waves. The extra cost is one indexed skill description, not necessarily the full body every session. Alternative: keep a short always-loaded policy in AGENTS and make `coordinate` the deep reference.

## Q5
Separate invariants from mechanisms. Host-neutral: one objective per worker, fresh state on disk, no re-deriving completed work, English reviewer briefs, no repository writes while agy/muse runs, ratings, and operator approval before skipping a required reviewer. Host-specific: subagents, scheduled wakes, `-Kick`, prompt-cache TTL, and auto-compaction. Phrase these as capability mappings: use a fresh isolated worker/session where supported; use `-Detach`/`-Status`/`-Wait` or an equivalent watchdog; compact or start fresh at wave boundaries before the host limit. Do not promise a universal prompt-cache TTL.

## Q6
Do not ship active worker definitions with pinned model names. Ship tier contracts: deep reasoning, default execution, cheap read-only recon. Let the host map tiers to models through a user-owned configuration generated at install time. If a host requires agent files, ship examples or generate them once, and never silently rewrite model names during upgrades. I need the target host's agent schema, mandatory model fields, alias stability, and upgrade ownership rules before choosing.

- RC1 (finding #1): workdir `<repo>`; permission workspace-write; in a throwaway HOME run `install-codex-host.ps1` with `CODEX_CONSULT_ROOT` unset, then `Test-Path` the referenced `scripts`, `schemas`, and `templates`; all must resolve or installation must fail loudly; budget 5 minutes.
- RC2 (findings #2-#3): workdir `<repo>`; permission read-only; inspect host identity markers and run a same-model/different-endpoint comparison; record the comparator and inference provenance; budget 20 minutes.
- RC3 (findings #4-#7): workdir `<repo>`; permission read-only; start a fresh hookless Codex session, delegate one wave, and request a detached watchdog; observe `coordinate` discovery and the wake/compaction mechanism; budget 15
